# Low TB 1 and TB 2 antigen-nil is associated with increased QuantiFERON Gold Plus reversions

**Authors:** Alexa Tabackman; Carlos Acuña-Villaorduña; Michelle Canning; Meagan Karoly; Madolyn R. Dauphinais; Robert Michaud; Tara C. Bouton; Daniel L. Bourque; Katherine A. Reifler; Vishakha Sabharwal; Katrina Traber; Akshay N. Gupte; Karen R. Jacobson; Pranay Sinha

**Affiliations:** 1Section of General Internal Medicine, Boston University Chobanian and Avedisian School of Medicine, Boston, USA | 2. Section of Infectious Diseases, Boston University Chobanian and Avedisian School of Medicine, Boston, USA | 3Boston Public Health Commission, Boston, USA | 4Boston University School of Public Health, Boston, USA | 5Boston Medical Center, Boston, USA | 6Section of Pediatric Infectious Diseases, Boston Medical Center, Boston, USA | 7Pulmonary Center, Boston University Chobanian and Avedisian School of Medicine, Boston, USA | 8.Department of Global Health, Boston University School of Public Health, Boston, USA

Dear Editor,

Interferon gamma release assays (IGRAs) are a mainstay for diagnosing latent tuberculosis infection (LTBI) in the United States. IGRAs offers significant advantages over skin tests including faster turnaround times and less susceptibility to subjective interpretation1. However, IGRAs are subject to variability due to factors such as manufacturing variations, timing and volume of blood collection, incubation and processing delays and immunomodulatory effects2-4. Reversion, where results change from positive to negative, has been observed among individuals undergoing serial IGRA testing5,6. Prior studies of the QuantiFERON-Gold assay have demonstrated higher rates of reversion among individuals with TB antigen-nil levels near the manufacturer suggested cutoff point of 0.35-0.7 IU/mL7,8. CDC guidelines from 2010 recommend that clinicians should consider repeating IGRA testing when results are borderline9.

The majority of prior studies investigating variability in IGRA tests have been conducted in healthcare workers in low-incidence settings.10-12. Few studies have investigated repeat testing in the broader population, including persons born outside of the U.S, or assessed the factors associated with reversion.

Our health system utilizes IGRA tests to detect LTBI in our diverse patient population, including routine screening for immigrants from high TB-burden countries, those with recent TB exposure, those requiring occupational health screenings, and individuals who are immunocompromised or undergoing immunosuppressive therapy. Identifying individuals with reversions could avoid costly and toxic LTBI treatment.

In April 2022, our TB clinic began repeating QuantiFERON Gold-Plus assays for individuals with a “borderline positive test” which we defined as TB1 and TB2 antigen-nil between 0.35-0.70 IU/mL. We did not offer LTBI treatment to those who underwent reversions. Since the meaning of these low positive tests is biologically uncertain, whether reflecting auto-clearance, false positives due to other exposures, or handling of the test, we did not extend this practice to patients with a higher risk of progression such as those with known TB exposure or severe immunocompromise defined as having HIV, end-stage renal disease, receiving chemotherapy or treatment with TNF-α inhibitors.

As part of a quality improvement project, we conducted a retrospective cohort analysis of patients who underwent more than one QuantiFERON Gold-Plus test at the Boston Medical Center/Boston Public Health Commission TB clinic between April 2018 (when the QuantiFERON Gold Plus assay was first adopted at our facility) and December 2024. Our goal was to assess the utility of our retesting threshold and identify factors associated with reversion. The cohort included individuals undergoing both routine testing external to our clinic and targeted repeat testing within our clinic. Patients >15 years with >1 QuantiFERON Gold-Plus test (Qiagen, Germantown, MD) were included, excluding individuals at high risk for disease progression as described previously. Given that data were collected through retrospective electronic medical record review for quality improvement purposes, IRB approval was not required.

Our primary outcome was reversion of QuantiFERON Gold-Plus and exposure was borderline positive test result. This range was selected based on prior literature 7,8. Covariates included age, sex, country of birth (dichotomized as U.S vs non-U.S), body mass index (BMI), interval of time between tests in days, and presence of comorbidities including chronic kidney disease (CKD), liver disease, alcohol use, tobacco use, diabetes and use of glucocorticoids.

We used univariate regression to identify factors associated with reversion and then built a multivariable model which included age, sex and country of birth a priori and variables with p < 0.2 in univariate analysis to determine the odds of reversion at TB1/TB2 ≤0.70.

261 patients were included in the analysis. The median age was 45 years and 96 (36.8%) were male. 46 (17.6%) were born in the United States. Reversion occurred in 61 (23.4%). In total, 112 patients (42.9%) had borderline positive tests, including 51 (88.5%) of those who reverted (Supplementary Table 1). The mean time between the two tests was 588 days (SD: 600 days). We did not find a significant difference in age or sex between those who reverted and who did not. A higher percentage of patients who reverted were U.S born (29.5% vs. 14.0%, p=0.01), and birth in the U.S (aOR 2.50, 95% CI 1.09-5.83) and TB1/TB2 ≤0.70 (aOR 18.00, 95% CI 7.66-49.14) were found to be associated with reversion (Table).

To assess for selection bias, we compared individuals with single QuantiFERON Gold-Plus testing to those with repeat testing. We did not find a significant difference in age or sex between these populations. A higher percentage of individuals who had repeat testing were born in the U.S (15.7% vs 10.9%). There was also a higher incidence of diabetes (16.9% vs. 12.2%) and CKD (3.4% vs. 2.7%) within the group that had repeat testing (Supplementary Table 2).

In summary, we found that TB1/TB2 ≤0.70 was associated with reversion along with birth in the U.S, a low TB incidence setting. Nearly half of individuals with borderline test results underwent reversions. Notably, our results show that even in those coming from high incidence TB settings, including Haiti, Vietnam, and Uganda, a significant number of reversions occurred. Individuals who revert from positive to negative may potentially avoid unnecessary treatment for LTBI, which is lengthy, costly, and carries toxicity risk including hepatoxicity, neuropathy, and drug-drug interactions13. That such a high rate of reversion was found even in a sample primarily born in high TB burden settings is striking and highlights need for more investigation. Although we have not conducted a longitudinal analysis, no participant left untreated due to a reversion progressed to TB disease to our knowledge.

Limitations of this study included variability in timing of repeat testing as this depended on when patients were referred to and seen in the TB clinic after an initial positive QuantiFERON Gold Plus test. Additionally, we noted a higher percentage of patients who were re-tested were born in the U.S, raising the possibility of selection bias among clinicians in selecting patients to repeat testing.

Our findings suggests that there is a role for repeat testing to assess for reversion in patients whose initial results fall within the borderline range of 0.35-0.70 IU/mL. As our findings reflect post-hoc associations, further prospective validation is needed to confirm the performance and cost-effectiveness of this re-testing threshold. Such research could open the door to more individualized care—future approaches could incorporate risk stratification to guide repeat testing in low-risk patients with borderline results, reducing unnecessary treatment, lowering costs, and enhancing person-centered TB care.
